content:
Since I've started to work on measure theory, I've had some ideas about various refactors, and I'd like to check that they wouldn't break anything important and that they fit with the spirit of the library.

  1. Move Mathlib.Dynamics.Ergodic.MeasurePreserving from Dynamics.Ergodic to MeasureTheory.Measure, so that it is alongside MeasurePreserving.

  2. Require QuasiMeasurePreserving and MeasurePreserving maps to be AEMeasurable instead of Measurable. It doesn't seem to affect e.g. MeasureTheory.MeasurePreserving.lintegral_comp.

  3. To allow this change, put QuasiMeasurePreserving downstream of the other files in MeasureTheory.Measure. As of now, quasimeasurepreserving maps are used in a rather silly way in the proof of MeasureTheory.NullMeasurableSet.mono_ac, which means they are upstream of MeasureTheory.Comap. That's easy to change.

  4. More generally -- but I may overstep -- there are many lemmas which have Measurable and AEMeasurable versions (or MeasurableSet and NullMeasurableSet versions). See for instance MeasureTheory.setLIntegral_indicator and MeasureTheory.lintegral_indicator₀. Outside of particular cases (simp lemmas...), why don't we just deprecate the Measurable version? Going from measurable to aemeasurable is easy, and this would remove many almost-duplicate lemmas.
For 2: the AEMeasurable version of MeasurePreservingalready exists. It's ProbabilityTheory.HasLaw

For 1: I think we intentionally moved the file from MeasureTheory to Dynamics before, so that should at least be discussed.
EDIT: I'm wrong, it was added there directly in this commit

@Rémy Degenne : Thanks for the information! That just changes the question, though -- is there any need for a separate QuasiMeasurePreserving notion, or does HasLaw suffice?

@Floris van Doorn What I would like to see is where Dynamics.MeasurePreserving is imported; I have the feeling that it gets mostly imported back into MeasureTheory or Probability files, which would justify the move. Is there any tool to check that?

I'm happy with your proposed change 4.
I think a lot of this is historical, since the measurable version came first.

I agree that the existence of HasLaw leaves many questions (should both exist? If yes, what about the very different names?) and I just wrote this quick answer because I don't have time for more right now.

Damien Thomine said:

Floris van Doorn What I would like to see is where Dynamics.MeasurePreserving is imported; I have the feeling that it gets mostly imported back into MeasureTheory or Probability files, which would justify the move. Is there any tool to check that?

If you just want to go 1-2 levels deep, it's in the top-right of the page of the Mathlib-docs you linked.
There are some dependency graph tools that would help if you want to have a deeper view, but I'd have to search for them on Zulip as well.

I agree with 4. Its a big refactor but I think the duplication has got out of hand.

I think HasLaw could be renamed to AEMeasurePreserving and in probability we can just use notation like X ∼[P] μ

Using notation does not make the name irrelevant: it still appears in every lemma name. I very much prefer the HasLaw name (at least in probability contexts), and I find that MeasurePreserving is a strange name when the two measures are different (edit, see explanation below:) of different nature in the informal context.

If it has any use in fields outside of probability such as ergodic theory (and I suspect it does) I find it a bit weird to use the probabilistic name for it (and of course I say this as a probabilist). I also think its weird to have the AE measurable version be called HasLaw and the measurable version be called MeasurePreservingThe name seems sensible to me since the measure (ENNReal number value) of each set is being preserved. This in particular has caused multiple people such as Damien (and at least one other but I cant find it) to be confused. Furthermore I recall @Etienne Marion said the following in a comment on this PR: #39503

"It took me a bit of time to decide whether HasLaw should be used systematically or not. But basically one rule is: if the function is measurable, then one should use MeasurePreserving because it is strictly stronger than HasLaw."

I wasn't sure if I agreed with this (though I didn't comment on it), but if we do use this convention then probability will end up using both for similar meanings and this will be even more confusing.

My preference would be for probability specifically to be allowed to use a convention that is (perhaps) not used anywhere else in the library and allow lemmas which are pretty clearly only about probability to use some alternative name in the lemmas (which may or not be abbrevs but should at least correspond with the use of some probability specific notation). I made this argument for lintegral being allowed to be called "expectation" in contexts where that is the main interpretation.

So I guess just to summarise my opinion, my preference order would be:

  1. AEMeasurePreserving, MeasurePreserving with special probability naming conventions and notation
  2. AEMeasurePreserving, MeasurePreserving with special notation but not special naming conventions
  3. AEHasLaw, HasLaw
  4. Status quo

I think if we do stick with 4 in my opinion to avoid some confusion we should perhaps then use HasLaw + a measurablity hypothesis always over MeasurePreserving in probabilistic contexts (in contrast to Etienne's comment).
I have also been confused before: #mathlib4 > integral_comp

David Ledvinka said:

  1. AEMeasurePreserving, MeasurePreserving with special probability naming conventions and notation

If we have AEMeasurePreserving and the notation X ∼[P] μ without the abbrev, it would not always pretty-print as we want, right? (unless we make a namespace for the notation)
I also wonder how this notation would look in the manual (in terms of which results display in notation, or none), which could be confusing for someone searching for lemmas.

I think that David's option 1 is not good because if we have a different way to refer to it in probability then we will have a mix of lemmas using the first name and lemmas with the second name, depending on whether it's a "probability lemma" or not, or more likely depending on whether the contributor who added it was working in probability or not. That means that you are never sure of how a lemma should be called, or that we have to add aliases for every lemma to make them findable in the other context.

I agree that it would be better to name both with the same name, like Name/AEName. I just dislike MeasurePreserving (and I understand that HasLaw is not great in ergodic theory or any field where the two measures play similar roles). Perhaps we need something more neutral?

But perhaps the Measurable version is mostly not useful as Damien suggests and could be deleted (with an explicit measurability hypothesis added in a few places), and we need only one name, whatever that good name is.

I think that reading that a function is MeasurePreserving between two measures makes it easy to guess what it means, while HasLaw sounds strange for me because in ergodic theory we do not think of the map f : α → α as a random variable
And I agree that having two different names is bad, as someone working in either field would likely name it after the version they are using.

Lua Viana Reis said:

a function is MeasurePreserving between two measures

And ergodic theory books also use this terminology for functions between two spaces or measures (like a factor map between two systems).

I don't like the name "measure preserving" because, as Rémy suggests, it does not preserves measures.

I think I know where this comes from. In ergodic theory, we like invariant sets, i.e; sets s such that f ''s ⊆ s. In practice, we use the more general Mapsto f s s, which has the same meaning, and haven't yet found a use for a more specialized notion.

Here, there is the same issue with measures. We like invariant or quasi-invariant measures (measures such that map f μ = μ), but use the more general MeasurePreserving f μ μ. The anomaly is to have used the restricted name (measure preserving) for a more general notion (measure morphisms).

Hence, a name change i probably warranted.
Anyone have suggestions for a neutral and better name then?
MapsMeasureTo? Or Measure.IsMappedTo?

Damien Thomine said:

Here, there is the same issue with measures. We like invariant or quasi-invariant measures (measures such that map f μ = μ), but use the more general MeasurePreserving f μ μ. The anomaly is to have used the restricted name (measure preserving) for a more general notion (measure morphisms).

Measure morphisms between different spaces are called measure preserving in the literature I have seen, and they are not restricted to "mapping a measure to itself". E.g. Tao's blog, the definition of factor maps in Einsiedler and Ward's book, Ergodic Theory via Joinings book, or any chapter introducing morphisms between ergodic systems in an ergodic theory book.
Probability theory does not use this term AFAIK.
I really don't think it should be changed, but MeasureHom sounds better than MapsMeasureTo

Damien Thomine said:

I don't like the name "measure preserving" because, as Rémy suggests, it does not preserves measures.

I don't agree with this at all. If you think of measures as being bundled into the space (which is reasonable especially since we use by volume_tac here), then docs#MeasureTheory.MeasurePreserving is exactly that a measurable function (or, to be precise, it's induced preimage function, which is the more natural thing in the context of measure theory) preserves the measure of a (measurable) set: μ (f ⁻¹' s) = ν s. I'm not sure how it could be named better. I wouldn't have found docs#ProbabilityTheory.HasLaw if my life depended on it.
I don’t think anyone claims that HasLaw is a good name outside of probability.

My argument is more "measure-preserving is an accurate description that agrees with the general literature on measure theory". The last sentence of my previous post could be omitted. In the same way, we use docs#MeasureTheory.ae even though in probability one often says "almost surely", and we use docs#Module instead of VectorSpace (although IIRC we might have a variable_alias for that now).
(deleted)

@Jireh Loreaux So, this is not really important, but I think there is a a gap in intuition, which might explain why Rémy or me are not comfortable with this vocabulary. With your (convincing) explanation, you see the transformation acting (covariantly) at the level of sets, and the measure of sets being preserved. Another intuition is to see directly the transformation acting at the level of measures (the intuition being that a measure is a "repartition of mass" and we move this mass around, without explicit reference to sets), in which case preservation would literally mean that the initial measure and the final measure are the same.

A useful comparison would be to isometries (distances-preserving maps). The first point of view (maps act at the level of points, and distance between points is preserved) is more or less the same. However, people tend not to push distances from one space to another in the same way, so the second point of view is AFAIK absent, and there is no conflict.

Anyway, that's not going to solve anything, but at least I think I see where the hangup might come from.
@Jireh Loreaux do you know some examples in the literature where the term 'measure-preserving' is used for maps which do not map a measure space into itself?

I think we're conflating two closely-related issues here. I see two issues with "measure-preserving" implying that the function is an endomorphism of a measure space:

  1. The function is implied to be an endomorphism. Jireh above convincingly argues that this is not really true.
  2. In the case of an endomorphism, the function is implied to preserve a single measure, rather than mapping a measure to another one.

A measurable function f from X to Y (measurable spaces) can naturally be viewed as inducing a map from measures on X to measures on Y. With this perspective, one can interpret 'f preserves A' as 'the pushforward of A under f is A'. Of course this only makes sense if the source and target (measurable) space are the same.

@Joris van Winden : Lua Viana Reis gave a couple of references before. That said, in ergodic theory, 95%+ of the time, a measure-preserving map is an endomorphism preserving a single measure. When this is not the case, the use of the "measure-preserving" for different measures borders on vocabulary abuse (note that we also see very often expressions like "T preserves the measure mu", which suggests that a measure-preserving map from (X, mu) to (Y, nu) doesn't preserve the measure mu...).

Ironically, probabilists are most likely the ones who most often use maps between spaces endowed with different measures (e.g. each time you "enrich the probability space" or "couple random variables"), but this is something hidden in the background with no specific term for it.

From my point of view the name MeasurePreserving is perfectly reasonable as soon as we see the two measures as similarly important and we see the function as a map between measure spaces. And for those uses HasLaw is a weird name.

My problem is with a very common case in probability where the two measures play very different roles. We use HasLaw (the a.e. version of MeasurePreserving) to say things like "X is a real standard Gaussian random variable". In that informal statement, one of the two measures is not even mentioned: it's some unspecified probability measure on the probability space, which could even change from line to line in the informal argument as we extend the space to add an independent random variable with some other distribution. MeasurePreserving in that context is strange.

Why not just call it MeasurePreserving and explain clearly in the docstring these caveats noted above? I'm not in the area so don't have an opinion about the name, I'm just suggesting a way forwards. I'm sure that group theorists would happily agree that a group homomorphism between different groups was multiplication-preserving, however my impression here is that there is a section of the community using the phrase"measure preserving" commonly in a narrower context and this is what is causing the discussion. My instinct is that a good docstring can solve this.

Well to me the issue is not there at all: calling measure-preserving a map between different spaces with different measures is perfectly fine. Using "measure-preserving" to say "X has an exponential law" is what is weird.

I know that it would be better if I could suggest a solution, but for now I don't have a better name for P.map X = Q that fits both contexts.
Can we export something to a different name, not just a different namespace?
Would it make sense to add a convention to only use HasLaw when the target measure is fixed? (and have HasLaw be an abbrev, so dot notation works)

I know that code duplication is bad. But in this specific situation the uses of HasLaw and MeasurePreserving (in its ae version) seem really different to me from a mathematical point of view, which is accurately reflected by the difference in the names. And the common API would be pretty small. So I think it would be reasonable to keep both notions, with the two names, add in their docstrings cross-references, a lemma saying that they're equivalent, develop the common API for one of them, and deduce it for the other one.

And then in probability theory everthing would use HasLaw, and in ergodic theory MeasurePreserving.
